questions.question: Picture a number line from −1 to 1. Each unit is cut into 4 equal parts, so there is a mark every 1/4 (0.25). Point A is at −0.75, three marks left of 0. Point B is at 1/2, two marks right of 0. Point C is at 1/4, one mark right of 0. Reading the marks from left to right, which list shows the three numbers from least to greatest?
questions.explain: Numbers grow from left to right, so a negative number is always less than any positive one: −0.75 < 1/4 < 1/2. A common trap is thinking 1/4 beats 1/2 because 4 is the bigger denominator; on the line 1/2 is two marks right of 0 while 1/4 is only one.

questions.question: Picture a number line from −1 to 1 with each unit cut into 10 equal parts, so there is a mark every 0.1. Three points are marked: −0.4, −1/2 and −1/5. The point −1/2 lands on the −0.5 mark and the point −1/5 lands on the −0.2 mark. Which list shows the points in order from farthest left to farthest right?
questions.explain: Change every number to the same form, −1/2 = −0.5 and −1/5 = −0.2; the farther left a point is, the smaller it is, so −0.5 < −0.4 < −0.2. Do not let the bigger denominator in 1/5 fool you: 1/5 is a smaller piece than 1/2, so −1/5 is closer to 0.

questions.question: Picture a number line from −1 to 1 with each unit cut into 8 equal parts, so there is a mark every 1/8 (0.125). Four points are marked: −0.5, −3/8, −1/4 and 1/8. Which point is farthest to the left, making it the least of the four?
questions.explain: Write each number in eighths: −0.5 = −4/8 and −1/4 = −2/8, so −0.5 is four marks left of 0, farther left than any other point. The trap is picking the negative with the smallest size, −1/4, as the least; for negatives, the bigger the size, the farther left it sits.

questions.question: Picture a number line from −1 to 1 with each unit cut into 10 equal parts, so there is a mark every 0.1. Four points are marked: −0.8, −1/2, −1/5 and −0.4. Which point is farthest to the right, making it the greatest of the four?
questions.explain: Turn the fractions into decimals, −1/2 = −0.5 and −1/5 = −0.2; the point closest to 0 on the left side, −0.2, is the greatest. Watch two traps: a bigger denominator does not make 1/5 a bigger piece, and −0.8 is not the greatest just because 0.8 is the biggest size.

questions.question: Order these rational numbers from least to greatest: −0.7, −2/3, −3/5, −1/2.
questions.explain: Rewrite everything in one form: −2/3 ≈ −0.667 and −3/5 = −0.6, then −0.7 < −0.667 < −0.6 < −0.5. The trap is swapping −2/3 and −3/5 because 5 is the bigger denominator; 3/5 is actually the smaller piece, so −3/5 is closer to 0.

questions.question: Four students in a Burnaby science class measured how much their model bridges dropped when a weight was placed on them. They recorded the changes in centimetres as −0.3, −1/4, −1/5 and −0.15. Which list orders the changes from least to greatest?
questions.explain: Change the fractions to decimals, −1/4 = −0.25 and −1/5 = −0.2, then order from most negative to least negative: −0.3, −0.25, −0.2, −0.15. Do not put −1/5 before −1/4 just because 5 is bigger than 4; fifths are smaller pieces than quarters.

questions.question: Which statement is true?
questions.explain: Put both numbers in the same form: −5/8 = −0.625, which is closer to 0 than −0.7, so −5/8 > −0.7. For negatives the bigger size is the smaller number, so −0.7 is less than −2/3 and −0.5 is less than −2/5; and 1/5 is a smaller piece than 1/4, so −1/5 is greater than −1/4.

questions.question: In a card game, a round can end with a negative score. Theo's scores for four rounds were: Round 1: −1/2, Round 2: −0.6, Round 3: −1/3, Round 4: −0.45. Which round gave Theo his highest score?
questions.explain: Write every score as a decimal: −1/2 = −0.5 and −1/3 ≈ −0.33, so −0.33 is closest to 0 and is the highest score. The trap is thinking 1/3 is bigger than 1/2 because 3 is the bigger denominator; thirds are smaller pieces than halves, so −1/3 is closer to 0 than −1/2.

questions.question: Four kids at a Kelowna pool drop toys that sink to different depths. Their heights compared with the water surface, in metres, are: Ava −0.75, Ben −3/5, Cara −1/2, Dev −2/5. Rank the toys from highest (closest to the surface) to lowest. Whose toy is second highest?
questions.explain: Convert to decimals: −0.4, −0.5, −0.6, −0.75; the number closest to 0 is highest, so Dev is first and Cara at −0.5 is second. Do not rank −2/5 below −1/2 because 5 is the bigger denominator; 2/5 = 0.4 is a smaller drop than 1/2 = 0.5.

questions.question: A weather station in Prince George records the change in snow depth each day for five days, in centimetres: −1/2, 0.3, 1/4, −0.7, −2/5. To find the median change, Sam must first put the five values in order. What is the median change?
questions.explain: Order the values first: −0.7, −1/2 (−0.5), −2/5 (−0.4), 1/4 (0.25), 0.3; the middle one is −2/5. The traps are taking the middle of the unordered list, or putting −2/5 left of −1/2 because 5 is the bigger denominator.

questions.question: Priya says −1/8 < −1/4. Her reason: 8 is bigger than 4, so 1/8 is the bigger piece, which pushes −1/8 farther left on the number line. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Nothing is wrong; a bigger denominator always means a bigger fraction
Her answer is right but her reason is not: 1/4 > 1/8, so −1/4 > −1/8
1/8 is smaller than 1/4, so −1/8 sits closer to 0 and is greater
Both numerators are 1, so −1/8 and −1/4 are equal; neither is less
questions.explain: Compare the sizes first: 1/8 = 0.125 is smaller than 1/4 = 0.25, so −1/8 is closer to 0 and −1/8 > −1/4. A bigger denominator means the whole is cut into more, smaller pieces, not a bigger fraction, and for negatives the bigger size is the smaller number.

questions.question: In a beanbag toss at a Surrey school fair, a throw that lands short of the line scores a negative distance. Ravi scored −0.4 m, Tia −1/4 m, Wes −0.35 m and Hana −3/8 m. Which list orders the players from the farthest short of the line to the closest to it?
questions.explain: Change the fractions to decimals, −1/4 = −0.25 and −3/8 = −0.375, then order from most negative: −0.4, −0.375, −0.35, −0.25. The trap is putting −3/8 first because 8 is the biggest denominator; 3/8 is a shorter distance than 0.4, so Hana is not the farthest short.
